title: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel
summary: Exfiltration over a command and control channel is the transfer of collected data out of a victim environment using the same communication path the adversary already uses to task and control implanted tooling. The mechanism matters because it removes a separate, conspicuous egress channel from the operation: the implant beacons to its controller, receives instructions, and returns results inside the same session, often over HTTPS to blend with ordinary web traffic but also over DNS, mail protocols, or a custom binary protocol on a non-standard port. Data is typically staged first, compressed and sometimes encrypted or encoded, then split into chunks that fit the profile of the carrier protocol, with the encoded bytes placed in request bodies, headers, URI parameters or DNS query names. Because command and control traffic is already expected to be periodic, exfiltration rides inside a pattern defenders must baseline before they can spot the change. The technique appears on endpoints, servers and cloud workloads alike, and the observable artefacts differ by vantage point. Network flow records show asymmetric byte counts, with outbound volume far exceeding inbound, across long lived sessions to the same destination. Web proxies and inspection logs show repeated uploads, unusual content types, large request bodies and consistent request sizes or timing. Name resolution logs show elevated query volume, long or high entropy subdomains and repeated queries to a single authoritative server. Endpoint telemetry captures the preceding collection and staging: archive creation, bulk file reads, access to database exports, clipboard or screen capture. Distinguishing malicious transfer from benign uploads requires context. Cloud synchronisation, update reporting, telemetry agents, backup replication and video conferencing all produce sustained outbound flows. Investigators therefore weigh destination reputation and age, whether the destination appears on any approved list, which process owns the connection, whether timing is machine regular, and whether the transfer coincides with staging activity on the same host.
objectives: Explain how an implant multiplexes command, control and data transfer over a single channel and why that complicates egress monitoring.
Interpret network flow asymmetries, long lived sessions and repeated upload patterns as candidate exfiltration rather than routine traffic.
Correlate endpoint staging artefacts such as archive creation and bulk file reads with outbound network volume on the same host.
Analyse name resolution carried transfer patterns using query volume, label entropy and authoritative server concentration.
Tune proxy, network detection and data loss prevention rules to reduce false positives from synchronisation, patch delivery and telemetry reporting.
Describe containment choices that stop the transfer without destroying evidence of the channel or the staged data.
